doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: The value of an educated listener and familiar material
summary: He prefers hearing great players on blues, rhythm changes and standards, and finds modern complex music hard to follow.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah. And I would be the same way too, I mean I often say, okay, let’s say I’m at a jazz festival and these guys all come back from the beyond for the greatest jam session ever. You know, it’s Coltrane, Sonn — well Sonny Rollins he’s here, so Sonny’s there and whatever, Johnny Griffin and George Coleman, all these cats, Dexter Gordon. And then the program starts and it’s five originals that I’ve never heard before and I can’t even figure out what the chord changes are. Would I enjoy that? No. What do I want to hear them play? Blues, rhythm changes and a couple of standards and see who can be the most creative on that very familiar format, or within that very familiar format. And I think that’s one of the things that made, or one of the real joys of being an educated jazz listener. You know historically speaking, knowing material before you hear it. Because then you have a frame of reference. You know you hear a guy do a tune that you’ve heard a million times before but he does it a little bit differently and then his improvisation has some magical things in it, harmonic substitutions, whatever, and like it’s a whole different tune. And it really allows you to appreciate what they’re doing even more. Because you’re listening from a position of knowledge rather than absolute ignorance. I mean I hear people play sometimes now, and I’m a musician, I’m a professional musician, and I have no idea what’s going on. I can’t tell what time signature they’re in, and I spend most of the time going like one, two, three, you know, figuring out, okay, they’re in thirteen. And then by the end of the tune, what is that, that’s like a weird, like a

major 7 flat 5, and then it goes down a minor third and it’s an inverted strange triad with a strange extension. And by the time I get to the end of the tune I’ve figured out a few chords and the time signature and I haven’t heard one thing that the people have played because I’ve spent the whole time trying to get my bearings so that I could understand it a little bit. And I don’t know how the casual listeners are reacting favorably to it because I can’t believe that they could be enjoying it as much as they seem to be.
